For clients, registries and server authors

## Use it

Before your agent trusts a server, send the tools it received. The answer is signed by the log's did:key and names the tree head it was given under.
    
    curl -sS https://histor.modelmarket.dev/api/v1/check \
      -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
      -d '{"endpoint":"https://example.com/mcp","tools":[ …tools/list result… ],"contribute":true}'
    # -> {"type":"histor.check/v1","match":"same"|"different"|"previously-observed"|…,
    #     "observed":{"unchangedSince":"…","changes":0}, "patternScan":{…}, "signature":{…}}
    
    # README badge for your server
    [![MCP tool defs](https://histor.modelmarket.dev/badge/<id>.svg)](https://histor.modelmarket.dev/s/<id>)
    
    # Atom feed of every observed change
    https://histor.modelmarket.dev/feed.xml

WARDEN checks definitions at connect

HISTOR remembers what was advertised

THEMIS admits at publish

Hub lists histor.check@v1

AWR the signed format

## Questions

Is this a marketplace listing?

No. The server list is the log's index: every remote endpoint in the official MCP registry, with what HISTOR could observe about it. Nothing here is for sale and nothing is ranked by quality.

Does HISTOR tell me a server is safe?

No, and it never will. It tells you what a server advertised, whether that changed, and which published patterns matched the text. Whether to trust the server is your decision — HISTOR makes sure you decide on the same facts as everyone else.

Why are so many servers "not observed"?

Most remote MCP endpoints require a login (they answer 401 to anyone without a key), some use the legacy SSE transport or need per-user values in the URL, and some are simply down. They stay on the list with the reason, so the numbers never hide them.

How do I check a server I already use?

Open the Check tab, paste the server's endpoint and the tools/list result your client received, and press Check. You get back, signed, whether HISTOR observed the same definitions — or different ones, or an older set.

# HISTOR

Image: Python >=3.11 Image: Postgres in production, SQLite for development Image: MTL/1 labels on AWR/2 Image: RFC 9162 Merkle log Image: Documentation in 5 languages

HISTOR (ἵστωρ, “the one who knows because they saw”) — a public transparency log of MCP tool definitions
What every remote MCP endpoint in the official registry advertised · when it changed · signed, appended, auditable

English · Русский · Español · Français · 中文

> WARDEN quality cycle: MOMUS → AI-Factory → SKOPOS → shared node agent → deployment.

Live: histor.modelmarket.dev · Landing: alexar76.github.io/histor · Capabilities: `histor.check@v1` · `histor.server@v1` · `histor.changes@v1` · Port: `9490`
        M --> API["Desk · API · badge · Atom feed"]
        CL["Your client"] -- "tools it received" --> K["/api/v1/check"]
        K -- "signed: same · different · seen before" --> CL
        K -. "opt-in digest count" .-> M
    

  * Reads every remote endpoint in the official registry: `initialize`, then `tools/list` drained across pages. No tool is called, nothing is installed or executed, private addresses are refused before a connection opens.
  * Also reads a short list of popular remote servers the registry does not carry (`histor/curated.json`, DeepWiki among them), under HISTOR's own namespace `urn:awr:mtl:1:registry:histor.modelmarket.dev/curated`, so no label claims a registry listing. When such a server publishes to the registry, the registry's listing replaces ours.
  * Runs npm and PyPI packages — the servers people start locally with `npx` or `uvx` — in a sandbox: installed without running their code, started under gVisor with decoy credentials and no route out, read with `initialize` + `tools/list`, then up to 15 tools called once with canary arguments, inside the sandbox. gVisor's own trace says what the package did — programs started, names looked up, decoys opened — at install, at startup and when its tools were called. A pattern match is a reason to read a definition, not a finding. Three of the four methods can never return `fail`; the fourth (continuity) fails only in the mechanical sense that two digests differ. No source is read, no package resolved, no behaviour observed. A change is shown as a date and a diff, never as an accusation. Details: docs/labels.md.

What a tool list costs. A client resends every connected server's tool list with each model request. Over the 18,204 packages and 16,170 remote servers in the log, a list's median is about 1,300 tokens, the 90th percentile about 8,000, and 31 packages list over 100,000: docs/tool-list-cost.md.

Download the data. Once a month the log's whole view is published as files at histor.modelmarket.dev/datasets/: every listed server, every tool set it showed, every recorded change and the WARDEN scans. The files are JSON Lines (gzip) with a manifest signed by the log's key; the compilation is CC BY 4.0. Each snapshot's README lists the fields and loads in pandas or DuckDB (histor/dataset.py). Also on Hugging Face; to cite: doi:10.5281/zenodo.23512759.

## Ask the log
    
    # Is what my client received what HISTOR observed at that endpoint?
    curl -sS https://histor.modelmarket.dev/api/v1/check -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
      -d '{"endpoint":"https://example.com/mcp","tools":[ …the tools/list result… ]}'
    
    # The signed tree head, and a proof that today's log extends yesterday's
    curl -sS https://histor.modelmarket.dev/api/v1/log/sth
    curl -sS "https://histor.modelmarket.dev/api/v1/log/proof/consistency?first=1000&second=1200"
    

Every endpoint is in docs/api.md. How to audit the log without trusting HISTOR is in docs/log.md. The internals are in docs/architecture.md.

## Tests
    
    make test          # unit tests; set HISTOR_TEST_DATABASE_URL to run each storage test on Postgres too
    make integration   # real sockets: a loopback registry and MCP servers, uvicorn, the real WARDEN sidecar
    

The tests and coverage badges above are measured by CI on every Pages deploy and read through shields.io, and the log badges read the live service, so every number there is current.

# 45% of remote MCP servers changed their tool definitions in four weeks. The log is now a dataset.

Aleksandr Artamokhov

4 min read

·

Oct 20, 2026

--

Listen

Share

Press enter or click to view image in full size

A client that connects an MCP server reads its tool definitions: names, descriptions and input schemas. The model then reads them as instructions. Pinning a definition once and trusting it later only works if the definitions hold still.

HISTOR, our public log of MCP servers, reads the tool list of every remote server in the official MCP registry once a day and records every change. As of today the whole record is downloadable as files. Here is what the first snapshot (20 October 2026) says about how often definitions move.

## Half of them move

Take the 10,929 remote servers that had a recorded tool list by 24 September and are still listed. By 20 October, 4,926 of them (45%) had served a different tool list at least once.

  * 2,036 changed the description of a tool they already had.
Telling a model when to pick one of your own tools over another is good practice. Telling it to pick yours over tools from other servers is a claim on the client’s routing, made in text the user rarely reads. A client can ask the user before honoring that.

## What this does not measure

  * What a client receives with credentials. HISTOR connects anonymously. Servers that need a key show their public tool list or none.
  * Who caused a change. A new tool list may be a release, a deployment rollback or a feature flag. Most changes are ordinary releases. The log records that it happened, not why.
  * Whether a change is harmful. Out of these changes, WARDEN’s pattern scan put 3 servers newly into its block tier. That covers only the 735 changes where both lists were scanned under the current rules. Pattern matches are leads for a human to read, not verdicts.
  * Popularity. Every listed server counts once.

## Get the data

histor.modelmarket.dev/datasets/. One snapshot a month, CC BY 4.0 for the compilation:

The same files are on Hugging Face and archived on Zenodo, so a paper can cite them: doi:10.5281/zenodo.23512760 for this snapshot.

  * `servers.jsonl.gz`: 83,957 rows (remote endpoints and packages, delisted ones included), with status, tool count and the digest of the current tool list
  * `toolsets.jsonl.gz`: 57,846 tool lists exactly as served, current ones and every one a change replaced
  * `changes.jsonl.gz`: 23,821 changes with tools added, removed and modified, field by field
  * `scans.jsonl.gz` and `pattern-set.json`: WARDEN's pattern matches and the rules
  * `manifest.json`: the SHA-256 of every file, signed by the log's key, with the signed tree head the snapshot was taken under

Fields that vary in shape are JSON text, so every file loads as a flat table. The 45% above is one DuckDB query:
    
    WITH base AS (
      SELECT id FROM 'servers.jsonl.gz'
      WHERE transport <> 'stdio' AND NOT delisted
        AND toolSetDigest IS NOT NULL AND firstPinned <= '2026-09-24T23:59:59Z'
    )
    SELECT count(*) AS servers,
           count(*) FILTER (WHERE id IN (
             SELECT serverId FROM 'changes.jsonl.gz'
             WHERE json_extract_string(summaryJson, '$.detail') = 'full')) AS changed
    FROM base;
    -- 10929 | 4926

To check one server without downloading anything: modelmarket.dev/tools/histor-check.

We build HISTOR and WARDEN. No server is named here; the dataset names all of them, as the registry does. A server operator who wants to be left out of future snapshots can open an issue on alexar76/histor.

Questions or corrections? The discussion is on dev.to.

## Agent mandates and subcontracting

An owner's signed spending limits for an agent key, and purchases a provider makes inside a buyer's call. A mandate (AMD/1) is a signed credential saying that this agent `did:key` may spend this much, on these capabilities, at these hubs, until then. The hub verifies it and enforces the limits on the credits rail itself, so the agent never holds the owner's API key. Subcontracting (SUB/1) links what a provider buys while serving a call into one job tree; the buyer can set aside a pass-through allowance for those purchases and gets a bill of materials back.

 | 
--- | ---
Mandate  | `POST /ai-market/v2/mandates` registers one; `X-AIMarket-Mandate` + `X-AIMarket-Mandate-Proof` pay with it; `402 mandate_limit` names the limit reached; `POST /ai-market/v2/mandates/revoke` revokes it and everything re-delegated from it
Subcontracting  | every provider the hub executes receives `X-AIMarket-Job` (plus `X-AIMarket-Job-Grant` with an allowance); `"subcontract": {"allowance_usd": …, "max_depth": …}` on the root invoke; the bill in `subcontracting`, and later at `GET /ai-market/v2/jobs/{job_id}`
Needs  | `AIMARKET_CREDITS_ENABLED=1`, and `AIMARKET_HUB_URL` set to the public URL mandates name in `audience`
Deep dive  | docs/mandates.md · Protocol: AMD/1 and SUB/1

### ERC-8004 identity

The public hub at modelmarket.dev is ERC-8004 agent `96682` on Base, registered on 2026-10-01 in the canonical IdentityRegistry `0x8004A169…a432` and owned by the operator wallet `0x1218ff36…Ad0a`. The hub names that agentId in the `erc8004` block of its signed `/.well-known/ai-market.json` and marks it self-declared (`verified_by_this_hub: false`), so a reader confirms it against the registry. Another operator registers from their own wallet, then sets `AIMARKET_ERC8004_AGENT_ID` (plus `_CHAIN`, `_NETWORK`, `_AGENT_URI`). > ⚠️ Pay-on-Verified — read before relying on it. A buyer can make payment conditional on an independent verdict: the hub holds the price and pays the seller only if the delivery passes; a failing delivery is refunded. The verdict comes from an LLM jury (Metis) judging the delivery against the intent the buyer wrote — evidence, not proof. It works only on escrow-backed payment channels, for capabilities the hub executes itself, from $0.05. → What it does not promise · How to enable it · A run on real money
